title: A Princeton deep reinforcement-learning controller steers DIII-D fusion plasmas clear of tearing instability; only two of the controlled shots disrupt
summary: A deep reinforcement-learning controller from Princeton kept DIII-D fusion plasmas below a tearing-instability threshold; all but one shot disrupted before it took control, and only two did after.
account: Researchers from Princeton University, the Princeton Plasma Physics Laboratory and partners trained a reinforcement-learning controller. Its training environment was built from a multimodal dynamic model that estimates the likelihood of future tearing instability, the leading cause of disruptions. They deployed it on DIII-D, the largest magnetic fusion facility in the United States, at General Atomics in San Diego. It adjusted total beam power and plasma triangularity to keep the estimated tearability under a threshold while maintaining high-confinement mode (H-mode) performance. It did so even at low safety factor and low torque. In the experimental session, discharges up to 193276 either had no reinforcement-learning control or tore before control started. Before reinforcement-learning control all shots except one were disrupted. Of the controlled discharges from 193277, only two (193277 and 193282) were disrupted. Average time-integrated normalized beta rose. The authors do not give the experiment dates. Nature received the manuscript on 12 July 2023, so the controlled shots took place before that day. Seo and colleagues published the results in Nature on 21 February 2024. Princeton Engineering's release of the same day says that the model could forecast tearing mode instabilities up to 300 milliseconds in advance. On 24 February 2024 the OECD AI Incidents Monitor logged the result as a positive outcome. No independent group has reported a test of this controller since.
purpose: The controller was built to avoid tearing instability while maintaining high-pressure plasma in DIII-D. The avoided disruptions were its intended use.
system: Deep reinforcement learning tearing-avoidance controller with a DNN tearability predictor (Keras model converted to real-time C)

deployer: DIII-D National Fusion Facility, General Atomics

data.answer:
An RL controller trained on a tearing-likelihood model kept DIII-D plasmas below the instability threshold; before RL control all but one shot disrupted, after it only two did (Nature, 21 Feb 2024).

This is a demonstrated experimental control capability, not electricity delivered to users or established commercial fusion performance. The abstract supports instability prevention under specified conditions, while the detailed discharge counts and 300-millisecond claim were not independently reanalyzed. Generalization to ITER remains prospective.

fields.title: A Princeton deep reinforcement-learning controller steers DIII-D fusion plasmas clear of tearing instability; only two of the controlled shots disrupt
fields.headline: AI from Princeton steers fusion plasmas clear of tearing instability

value.role: SHA-256 of the complete public record and its assessments

fields.account: Researchers from Princeton University, the Princeton Plasma Physics Laboratory and partners trained a reinforcement-learning controller. Its training environment was built from a multimodal dynamic model that estimates the likelihood of future tearing instability, the leading cause of disruptions. They deployed it on DIII-D, the largest magnetic fusion facility in the United States, at General Atomics in San Diego. It adjusted total beam power and plasma triangularity to keep the estimated tearability under a threshold while maintaining high-confinement mode (H-mode) performance. It did so even at low safety factor and low torque. In the experimental session, discharges up to 193276 either had no reinforcement-learning control or tore before control started. Before reinforcement-learning control all shots except one were disrupted. Of the controlled discharges from 193277, only two (193277 and 193282) were disrupted. Average time-integrated normalized beta rose. The authors do not give the experiment dates. Nature received the manuscript on 12 July 2023, so the controlled shots took place before that day. Seo and colleagues published the results in Nature on 21 February 2024. Princeton Engineering's release of the same day says that the model could forecast tearing mode instabilities up to 300 milliseconds in advance. On 24 February 2024 the OECD AI Incidents Monitor logged the result as a positive outcome. No independent group has reported a test of this controller since.
